Bankers Still Sound Cautious About AI Boom
 
Plus, China’s auto industry crashes at home and airlines come up short on futuristic perks
 
 
GILLES SABRIÉ
 

China has reported robust growth this year, despite a continuing crash in its property market and consumer spending that is largely at a standstill. That is stirring questions that have long dogged China’s official data: Are the numbers accurate?

 

Opaque collection methods and concerns about political influence have for years cast doubts on Beijing’s economic data. But as the country grapples with a persistent slowdown that doesn’t always show up in government figures, that skepticism is growing louder.

 

Estimates from some Western analysts for China’s full-year growth range from 0% to 3%, far lower than the 4.5% expansion Beijing reported for the third quarter. Moreover, several prominent economists in China are arguing that the unemployment rate—which edged down to 5.2% in September, according to government figures—masks a more serious jobs crisis.

 

Below, some of the best analysis and insight from WSJ writers and columnists, the Dow Jones Newswires team and occasionally beyond, on investing, the wealth-management business and more.

 
 
 

Planning & Investing

 

AI Boom Drives a Jump in Lending, but Bankers Still Sound Cautious

 

In the third quarter, both big banks and midsize regionals reported sharp jumps in their traditional business-loan books, known in the industry as commercial-and-industrial lending. The AI data-center build-out was often cited as a driving force.

 
 
 

Market Talk

 

From Dow Jones Newswires

 

Treasury Chief John Healey has bought himself time rather than resolving the U.K.’s fiscal problems, Sanjay Raja at Deutsche Bank says in a note. Although markets reacted positively to the budget, borrowing is expected to remain higher than previously forecast, while much of the promised fiscal tightening is backloaded, raising questions about whether it will be delivered, he says. The tax burden is still on course to reach a postwar high, despite limited new tax increases, and further spending pressures are looming including defense and social care, Raja says. “Put simply, there will be a near GBP25-40 billion fiscal hole to fill in the new year… the U.K. is walking an increasingly fine fiscal line, with the harder choices still to come,” he says. (don.forbes@wsj.com)

 

The Bank of Canada’s decision to raise the policy rate shows the balance of risks has now tipped toward the threat of energy-driven inflation over downside risks from trade tensions, Capital Economics’ Bradley Saunders says. Still, the economist says the central bank pushed back against hawkish market pricing which supports his view that the tightening cycle will be limited to two more rate increases next year. The bank in its decision says a high degree of uncertainty means it will proceed carefully, though there could be a need to raise rates further. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)
